hanke-make-in-india-25pct-target-vs-16pc:
Manufacturing's place in India's economy is roughly where it was twelve years ago.
The target set in 2014 was a quarter of the economy, and no statistical series in use today puts it anywhere near that line.

@@REF@@Net assessment of India's manufacturing sector (Ideas for India, 2026-02-27)|https://www.ideasforindia.in/topics/macroeconomics/net-assessment-of-indias-manufacturing-sector

That figure did not originate with the Modi government.
The National Manufacturing Policy of 2011 had already written down a goal of lifting manufacturing to 25% of the economy within a decade while creating 100 million jobs,
and the Make in India campaign of 2014 adopted that same number as its own.

## Fifteen percent or sixteen, depending on the ruler

The "15% or below" in Hanke's post is a number that moves with the ruler you pick.

Measured as gross value added, the series India's own statistics office publishes, manufacturing has drifted between 16% and 18%.
Measured as a share of gross domestic product, the basis the World Bank uses so countries can be compared, it falls to around 12%.
The two rulers differ over where taxes and subsidies are added or removed, and over which year is used as the price base.

@@BAR@@2014 government target|25%|25|India statistics office, GVA basis (2024-25)|16.3%|16.3|World Bank, GDP basis (2024)|12.5%|12.5@@Neither ruler reaches two thirds of the target line. Hanke's "15% or below" holds only on the World Bank basis; on the one India's own government uses, the figure is in the sixteens.@@Retrieved 2026-08-17 · India's new national accounts series (2022-23 base, constant prices) and World Bank NV.IND.MANF.ZS

## Why the factories grew and the share did not

This is where the reading usually goes wrong.

A flat share does not mean manufacturing failed to grow.
Manufacturing output itself has expanded at roughly 6% a year since 2021.
Services simply expanded at close to 8% over the same stretch.

A share is a fraction.
When the numerator grows and the denominator grows faster, the ratio falls.

Not everything can be blamed on the denominator, though.
Of 23 manufacturing sub-sectors, 11 produced less in 2024-25 than they did in 2018-19.
The aggregate rose because a handful of sectors carried the rest.

## The iPhones really were built in India

A stalled share does not mean the policy changed nothing.

The Production Linked Incentive scheme, launched in 2021, committed 1.97 trillion rupees, about $22.8 billion, across 14 sectors.
Investment actually realised through March 2025 was counted at 1.76 trillion rupees.

@@REF@@Apple's iPhone exports from India hit a record $10 billion in FY25 (Business Standard, 2025-10-08)|https://www.business-standard.com/india-news/apple-iphone-exports-india-record-10-billion-fy25-tata-foxconn-125100800643_1.html

According to that report, Apple's vendors assembled $22 billion worth of iPhones in India in fiscal 2025,
and roughly 80% of that, some $17.5 billion, was shipped abroad.
Foxconn and Tata Electronics divide the volume between them.

The gap is in the size of the board.
Incentives actually disbursed over the same period came to 215 billion rupees, about 11% of the money set aside.
The promise was large and the execution was small.

## What the early-2027 national accounts settle

@@CMP@@Hanke's reading|Twelve years and the share has not moved a notch. It cleared barely half the target, so the policy failed.|New Delhi's reading|Manufacturing output grew about 6% a year. The share stalled because services grew faster.

Both sides are looking at the same twelve years; one reads a numerator that would not grow, the other a denominator that grew faster.

The dispute matters because it splits how an investor can own Indian manufacturing.
One way assumes the target eventually gets filled and buys Indian industry broadly.
The other ignores the share entirely and buys only the narrow boxes where volume genuinely rose, electronics and semiconductors.
The record of the last twelve years favours the second.

The point of decision is the next set of national accounts.
If the provisional estimate for fiscal 2026-27, due early in 2027, puts manufacturing above 17.5%, the stall is over; below that line, it is a thirteenth year in the same place.
serenity-stripe-openrouter-7b-routing-la:
Reports on August 16 said the payments company Stripe had agreed to buy OpenRouter for more than $7 billion.
Bloomberg had it first, and neither company has confirmed anything.

@@REF@@Stripe will reportedly acquire AI gateway startup OpenRouter for $7B+ (TechCrunch, 2026-08-16)|https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/16/stripe-will-reportedly-acquire-ai-gateway-startup-openrouter-for-7b/|https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Stripe-resized.webp?resize=1200,674

OpenRouter does not build AI models.

## What a company that builds no models actually does

@@FLOW@@A developer's app|Connects to OpenRouter once|OpenRouter|Decides which of 400-plus models the request goes to|The model companies|OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others do the actual computing|The fee|Model prices pass straight through, with roughly 5% added on top@@What OpenRouter holds in this path is not computing power. It is the seat where the choice of model gets made.

Wiring AI into an app normally means connecting to each provider separately.
Once to OpenAI, once to Anthropic, once to Google.

OpenRouter collapses that into one connection.
The developer integrates a single time, and OpenRouter decides where each request goes.
If one provider goes down, traffic moves to another.

The company was founded in New York in 2023 and is run by Alex Atallah, a co-founder of the NFT marketplace OpenSea.

## Three weeks took $3 billion off the price

@@BAR@@Valuation at the May 2026 funding round|$1.3B|13|Reported acquisition price|$7B|70@@More than fivefold in three months. OpenRouter did not build a new model in that stretch. What grew was the volume of requests passing through the layer.@@Retrieved 2026-08-17 · Series B valuation of 2026-05-26 (TechCrunch) · acquisition price as reported 2026-08-16 (Bloomberg, TechCrunch, Fortune)

A different number was circulating in late July.
The Wall Street Journal reported on July 23 that Stripe was in talks at around $10 billion.
Three weeks later the reported figure was over $7 billion.

@@REF@@Stripe clinches over $7 billion deal to buy AI firm OpenRouter (Fortune, 2026-08-16)|https://fortune.com/2026/08/16/stripe-7-billion-deal-ai-firm-openrouter-acquisition/|https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-2147863391-e1786918883496.jpg?resize=1200,600

Fortune added that the final price could still change.
Nothing was taken away from OpenRouter in those three weeks.
What was marked down was the price of how defensible this middle layer is.

## Where Serenity puts the pressure

Serenity's view is that this orchestration layer is easy to replicate and easy to switch away from, so there is very little moat.
What OpenRouter does hold right now, he adds, is the user base, the accumulated data and the momentum.

Others already do the same job.
Vercel and Cloudflare each ship a gateway, and there is open-source software anyone can pick up.
Moving off it means rewiring integrations, which costs weeks rather than years.

## The books Stripe was already reading

There is one thing the post does not mention.

OpenRouter has been billing its own customers through Stripe since January 2026.
That means Stripe could see what this company collects and how fast it is growing from the payment ledger rather than from outside estimates.
Stripe also co-wrote, with OpenAI, a protocol for letting AI agents pay on a person's behalf.
What is being bought here is not a model. It is the point where money crosses into AI.

## It comes down to whether an announcement lands by year-end

Everything so far is sourced reporting, and Stripe's line is that it does not comment on rumors.
If the acquisition is announced by year-end, the negotiation that took $3 billion off in three weeks stays part of what the price means.
If the year closes with no announcement, the price on this layer has not been settled yet.

The expensive thing in AI is supposed to be the model.
What got a price this time was not the model. It was the toll booth standing in front of it.
hanke-boj-september-hike-m2-2_2pct-cpi-1:
Markets expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates once more in September.
Reuters reported on August 14 that the bank is weighing a September hike and a faster pace of tightening,
and that markets were pricing in nearly an 80% chance of a move that month.

@@REF@@BOJ eyeing September rate hike, faster pace of tightening, sources say (Reuters, 2026-08-14)|https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/boj-eyeing-september-rate-hike-061747472.html|https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/14711F721D04BFFED2AC8A2874B33CB3FEEA0C21B09C5052263DEFD8E9E2C80E/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w1200_h840;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Freuters.com%2F2912e5c407ebcad939a6af2e96caa6f7.jpg

The two numbers usually cited as grounds for a hike are both sitting under target.

## Money is growing slowly and they are tightening anyway

@@CHK@@Policy rate|1.00%|Money stock (M2), year on year|2.2%|Core CPI, year on year|1.6%@@Both numbers a hiker would normally lean on point the wrong way. Money is growing slower than the 2.6% average for 2000 to 2020 that Hanke cited in his July column, and core inflation has been under the 2% target for five straight months. His premise, that tightening is not what Japan needs right now, checks out in the data.@@Retrieved 2026-08-17 · Bank of Japan, Money Stock preliminary figures for July 2026, released 2026-08-12 · Statistics Bureau national CPI for June · Bank of Japan policy statement of 2026-07-31

@@REF@@Japan June core inflation accelerates, stays below BOJ target (Reuters, 2026-07-23)|https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/japan-june-core-inflation-accelerates-010629443.html|https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/8E706363DF91D798C7BD593BB0BCB4A4813D4628639D827BFAD7433AD8317BEC/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w1200_h830;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Freuters.com%2Faa949fdce46032737cf57619df59074d

Reuters reported that core inflation rose to 1.6% in June from 1.4% in May while still coming in under the 2% target for a fifth month.
The national figure for July has not been published yet.

The money stock is simply the total amount of money circulating in an economy.
M2 counts the part of it people can spend right away, cash and deposits,
and when that number grows slowly it means there is less force available to push prices up.

Raise rates from here and money that was already growing slowly grows slower still.
That is why Hanke wrote that more tightening is exactly what Japan does not need.

## So what are they looking at instead

@@TIME@@2025-01-24|Hike from 0.25% to 0.50%, the highest since 2008|2025-12-19|Hike to 0.75%, the highest since 1995|2026-06-16|Hike to 1.00%|2026-07-31|Held at 1.00%, with one board member arguing for 1.25%|>2026-09-18|Next policy meeting@@Eighteen months took the rate from 0.25% to 1.00%. A fourth hike is hanging on September.@@Retrieved 2026-08-17 · Bank of Japan policy statements, English releases

What has moved is not the price data. It is the yen.

Japan intervened alongside the United States last month, and the yen was still at 159.1 to the dollar on August 11.
A cheaper yen makes imported goods dearer, and that cost reaches consumer prices with a lag.
At his late-July press conference Governor Ueda said the effect of currency swings on inflation may be larger than it used to be.
In the same appearance he said underlying inflation is nearing 2% and that the bank must watch upside risks in a way it did not before.

## Wages cleared 5% for a third year

The other input is pay.
Rengo, Japan's trade union confederation, finalized this year's spring wage round on July 3 at an average increase of 5.01%, the third consecutive year above 5%.

@@REF@@Japan Unions Clinch 5.01 Pct Wage Hikes in 2026 Shunto (Jiji Press via nippon.com, 2026-07-03)|https://www.nippon.com/en/news/yjj2026070300852/japan-unions-clinch-5-01-pct-wage-hikes-in-2026-shunto.html

Rising pay gives households more to spend, and that spending lifts prices. This is the picture the bank has waited years to see.
It has not shown up in the price data yet.

@@CMP@@Hanke's reading|Money is already growing at just 2.2% a year. Tighten from here and you shrink the force that could lift prices at all.|The bank's reading|Core inflation is still low, but a weak yen and a third year of 5% pay rises will push prices up from here.

Two readings of one meeting. One is looking at money that is already circulating slowly, the other at inflation that has not arrived.

## September 18 answers it

If the meeting on September 17 and 18 takes the rate to 1.25%, the bank will have moved on the currency and on wages rather than on realized inflation.
The next question then shifts to the money stock: whether money growing at around 2% a year can keep supporting a third straight year of 5% pay increases.

If the bank holds instead, five months of below-target inflation will have beaten the 80% the market priced in.
Attention then moves to the July national CPI due on August 21.

Raising rates in a country where money circulates slowly looks less like an act of price control
and more like an act of currency defense.
meru-china-dried-laver-seasoning-value-c:
China is buying roughly twice as much Korean dried laver as it did two years ago.
Figures released by Korea's Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries on August 16 show shipments to China rising from 2,543 tons in 2024 to 4,539 tons in 2025,
with 2,416 tons already gone in the first half of this year.

@@REF@@China moves up the value chain in South Korea's “black semiconductor” boom (KED Global, 2026-08-17)|https://www.kedglobal.com/economy/newsView/ked202608160004|https://www.kedglobal.com/data/ked/image/2026/08/16/ked202608160024.jpg

The odd part is that China grows more laver than any other country on earth.

## Chinese laver cannot become a seasoned sheet

Laver comes in species, and the species decides what it can become.
Most of what China farms is the warm-water variety Pyropia haitanensis.
It grows where the sea is too warm for anything else, but the sheet it makes is thick and chewy,
so it ends up in soup rather than in the thin roasted sheets sold as a snack.

Korea and Japan farm Pyropia yezoensis, which is the opposite.
It grows only in cold water and comes out thin enough that oil, salt and a pass over heat give you the brittle sheet most people picture when they think of seasoned laver.

That is the first reason China buys Korean dried laver.

Meru offers a different reason.
Chinese coastal water, he writes, is polluted badly enough to keep the product out of export markets.
China's own published numbers point the other way.

@@CHK@@Coastal water rated good, 2024|83.7%|Coastal water rated poor, 2024|8.6%|Rated good, 2023|85.0%@@A number close to 84% does turn up. It is the share of coastal water rated good, not the share failing the standard. Pollution on its own looks like a weak explanation for why China buys Korean dried laver.@@Retrieved 2026-08-17 · China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment, 2024 national bulletin published 2025-06-04, as summarized by China Water Risk

There is a real research literature on heavy metals, cadmium in particular, off the Jiangsu coast.
What the official bulletin does not support is the wider claim that the coastline as a whole cannot grow export-grade laver.

## The money sits in the seasoning step

@@BAR@@Dried laver, bundle of 100 sheets|8,500 won|8500|Seasoned laver, same bundle|25,000 won|25000@@It is the same seaweed. One step, brushing it with oil and salt and toasting it, nearly triples the price. China buys at the first number and sells at the second.@@Retrieved 2026-08-17 · Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries data of 2026-08-16, as reported by the Korea Economic Daily

Chinese processors import Korean dried sheets, brush them with oil and salt in the Korean style,
print a Korean-language brand on the package and ship them out again.
The raw material is Korean, so the taste barely differs, and the price is lower.

Seasoned laver has fallen from 43.2% of Korea's laver export volume in 2020 to 35.3% in 2025.
Over those same five years the volume of dried laver Korea exports rose 82%.
Korea is selling more and keeping less of what each sheet is worth.

## Washington waived the tariff on the seasoned kind

@@REF@@Seasoned gim exempt from US tariff (The Korea Times, 2025-12-14)|https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/business/companies/20251214/seasoned-gim-exempt-from-us-tariff|https://newsimg.koreatimes.co.kr/2025/12/14/97ad6446-f4be-4867-aad8-a4be4973bfa5.jpg

On November 13, 2025 the United States dropped the 15% tariff it charged on seasoned laver.
Dried laver still carries the 15%.

Korea sold $228 million of laver into the United States through November last year, roughly 90% of it seasoned,
and the United States takes about a fifth of Korea's laver exports.
Total laver exports through the same month came to $1.04 billion, the first time the figure has passed a billion dollars in a year.

The step where the price triples and the step where the tariff disappeared are the same step.
If Chinese processors fill it, what is left for Korea is supplying the input.

## What the early-2027 numbers will settle

In June the ministry published a supply-chain plan for laver exports built around a “Made in Korea” national certification mark.
The point of the mark is to separate Korean seasoned laver from Chinese product wearing a Korean-language label,
and the plan carries a target of $1.8 billion in exports by 2030.

If the mark creates a real distinction on American shelves, the seasoned share climbs back.
If the 2026 annual figures instead put it below 35.3%,
Korea has slid one more step from selling the finished good toward selling the input.

In the year laver exports first passed a billion dollars, the question worth asking is not how much Korea sold.
It is which step Korea sold.
meru-korea-cpi-housing-weight-9_91pct-vs:
Seoul apartment prices rose 13.5% over one year.
Over the same stretch, Korea's consumer price index rose 2.8%.

@@REF@@Seoul small apartments lead price surge amid loan curbs (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-07-23)|https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/07/23/seoul-small-apartments-lead-price-surge-amid-loan-curbs|https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/07/23/news-p.v1.20260722.299beed5316d4458b7919afcf35743ce_P1.png

The reason the two numbers diverge this far is simple.
Korea's consumer price index has no line for house prices at all.

What an index does not count did not happen as far as the index is concerned.

## How a price index counts a home

The only housing components in the Korean index are jeonse and monthly rent.
Jeonse carries a weight of 5.4% and monthly rent 4.5%, and together they do not reach 10%.

The United States counts it differently.
Homeowners are asked what their house would fetch if they rented it out, and that figure goes into the index.
This is called owners' equivalent rent: in plain terms, the rent you are treated as paying yourself to live in your own home.

@@BAR@@Housing rent in Korea's consumer price index|9.9%|9.91|Shelter in the US consumer price index|35.6%|35.6@@Two indexes with the same name give housing this much difference in space. Narrowed to core inflation, the US figure rises to 44.5%.@@Statistics Korea 2026 CPI weights · US Bureau of Labor Statistics relative importance table, December 2025 · retrieved 2026-08-17

When house prices rise, the American index records at least part of it through rental value.
The Korean index has no box for it, so it records nothing.

## And what it does record, it records late

Jeonse and monthly rent contracts usually run two years.
Statistics Korea surveys not only newly signed contracts but the entire stock of existing ones.

So even when market rents rise, the index does not move until renewals come around.
Today's rent increases show up in inflation one to two years from now.

## The tap opened on August 13

@@FLOW@@Double the household lending cap|The annual growth target for bank household loans went from 1.5% to 3.0%|Move balance and interim payments outside it|Taking those loans out of the volume cap widened the real headroom further|About 30 trillion won added|Money that buys homes rather than goods and services|The index stays quiet|House prices are not a component, so the end of this path never reaches the inflation figure@@The last box in this path is the point of the piece. What matters is not where the money goes but whether its destination is something the index measures.

@@REF@@Korea doubles the household loan growth target to 3% (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-08-13)|https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/08/13/korea-doubles-2025-household-loan-growth-target-to-3|https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/08/13/news-p.v1.20260806.cf902aeb0974402e9d7df7646d865e63_P1.jpg

Behind the measure was congestion at the lending window.
The five major banks blew through their annual quotas in July, leaving roughly 70,000 households due to move into new apartments in the second half struggling to get balance-payment loans, and queues formed outside branches before dawn.

The package also contains a clause pulling the other way.
Guarantee ratios on jeonse loans for owners who live away from the home they own were cut from 80% to 70% in Seoul to push them into occupying it, which shrinks the pool of homes offered for lease.
That is the clause the Hyundai Research Institute singled out when it put second-half inflation at 2.7% and said it could reach 3% if the risks materialize.

## What the Bank of Korea faces on August 27

The Bank of Korea held rates eight meetings in a row and then raised the base rate by 25 basis points on July 16.
It was the first hike in three years, and the dot plot published afterwards had 10 of the 21 board members at 3.0% by year-end.

The financial regulator is releasing credit so genuine buyers can close on their apartments, while the central bank has to restrain the debt and the house prices that credit creates.
Two arms of the same state are now pulling in opposite directions.
Household debt is already estimated to have passed 2,000 trillion won for the first time.
The absence of house prices from the index works against the Bank of Korea in this standoff.
Quiet measured inflation weakens the case for raising rates, while asset prices and debt keep growing outside what that quiet measure covers.

So the place to watch is the rent index from August onward.
If the base rate reaches 3.0% or higher by year-end, the side effects of the August 13 package moved monetary policy; if it stays where the July hike left it, the gap between the two institutions never showed up in the rate.
semianalysis-pjm-reserve-model-3_8gw-vs-:
The largest electricity market in the United States will hold an auction from September 30 to buy more power plants.
An analysis now argues that this market is undercounting the generating capacity it already has by 3.8 gigawatts.

@@REF@@PJM files backstop auction plan at FERC to meet capacity shortfall (Utility Dive, 2026-08-03)|https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-backstop-capacity-auction-ferc-data-centers/826792/|https://imgproxy.divecdn.com/9mc3NVqI62Ic8RIYSCYVrATgz4o1J-WyWFfhCuMzTfM/g:ce/rs:fit:770:435/Z3M6Ly9kaXZlc2l0ZS1zdG9yYWdlL2RpdmVpbWFnZS9HZXR0eUltYWdlcy0yMTYxODUwNjkxXzEuanBn.webp

PJM runs the grid that serves 13 states and Washington, DC, home to 66 million people.
Electricity bills there have risen between 10% and 25% over the past year depending on the state.

SemiAnalysis argues that a large share of that increase is the product of an arithmetic error.

## There is a separate market for buying power plants

What changes hands in this auction is not electricity but readiness.
Generators are paid in advance to stand available for the moment they are needed, and that arrangement is called a capacity market.

Think of it as paying for a fire station.
The trucks and crews cost money every year whether or not a fire breaks out.

So the price in this market is set not by the electricity actually consumed but by how large a shortfall the operator calculates.

## Power plants get stronger in winter

A gas plant produces more electricity in cold air.
Cold air is denser, so the same turbine can push out up to 25% more power.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Gas_stove_blue_flames.jpg/500px-Gas_stove_blue_flames.jpg|The asset at the center of this card. The same plant generates more electricity in midwinter than it does in summer.|Marina Burity · CC BY-SA 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gas_stove_blue_flames.jpg

There is a second piece.
After Winter Storm Elliott knocked out 13% of Eastern Interconnection capacity at once in December 2022, roughly 400 of PJM's approximately 700 gas plants spent money on winterization.

SemiAnalysis argues that PJM's model still reflects neither of these.
Counting them, the firm estimates, would put 3.8 gigawatts more on the system, the equivalent of eight large gas plants.

## Who the bill for the increase was addressed to

@@CHK@@Total cost of the last four capacity auctions|$63.6 billion|Share the market monitor attributes to data centers|$29.4 billion|Clearing price, 2028/29 auction|$333.44 per MW-day@@Data centers have already been named as the culprit behind rising bills, and their share is close to half. The modeling problem SemiAnalysis points to is a candidate for explaining the other half.@@Monitoring Analytics, PJM's independent market monitor, as reported by Utility Dive 2026-07-20 · PJM 2028/29 Base Residual Auction results · retrieved 2026-08-17

@@REF@@Data centers drove $6.3B in PJM capacity auction costs, market monitor says (Utility Dive, 2026-07-20)|https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-data-centers-capacity-auction-imm-bowring/825626/|https://imgproxy.divecdn.com/oSOhdb7tT_-vuiArR7FEl0Exy4T6Odfupucyli8Mb9Q/g:ce/rs:fit:770:435/Z3M6Ly9kaXZlc2l0ZS1zdG9yYWdlL2RpdmVpbWFnZS9TY3JlZW5zaG90XzE5OC5wbmc=.webp

The market monitor calculated that 38% of the cost of the 2028/29 auction was driven by data centers.
PJM itself forecasts that 30 of the 32 gigawatts of peak demand growth through 2030 will come from data centers.

The two explanations do not exclude each other.
Demand really is growing quickly, and undercounting supply on top of that makes the gap look bigger than it is.

## The auction on September 30 supplies the answer

@@TIME@@December 2022|Winter Storm Elliott takes out 13% of Eastern Interconnection capacity|December 30, 2024|Pennsylvania's governor files a complaint at FERC over the auction design|July 31, 2026|PJM files its emergency auction plan at FERC|>September 30, 2026|The emergency auction opens@@The argument over these bills is now in its fourth year on the same grid. So far it has been conducted in assertions; this auction answers in prices.@@Utility Dive and American Public Power Association reporting · retrieved 2026-08-17

PJM intends to procure 6.8 gigawatts in this emergency auction.
The 3.8 gigawatts SemiAnalysis believes are already there would cover more than half of that.

The auction signs 15-year contracts, and the price cap has been raised to $555 per MW-day.
Its weak link is that no large customer has yet committed to pay for the power.
If the contracts are signed and no buyer for that electricity appears, the cost lands back on residential bills.

So the clearing price due on December 2 is the first scorecard in this argument.
If it runs all the way to the $555 cap, the shortfall is real rather than a modeling artifact; if it settles below the cap, there was slack on the system that nobody had counted.
serenity-sandisk-lta-two-thirds-of-2028-:
Two-thirds of the NAND SanDisk will make in 2028 has already been sold.
Who buys it, and at what price, is written into the contracts.

@@REF@@SanDisk lays out long-term supply agreements with eight customers and FY2028-2030 targets at its investor day (SanDisk Newsroom, 2026-08-13)|https://www.sandisk.com/company/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2026-08-13-sandisk-investor-day-2026|https://www.sandisk.com/content/dam/sandisk/en-us/assets/company/newsroom/press-release/2026/inv-day26.png

What used to decide a memory maker's year was the spot price of the day.
Earnings rose when prices rose and fell when they fell, which is why this business has long been the textbook example of a cyclical one.

What changed is not the price but the way the price is set.

## Where NAND actually ends up

NAND is the chip that holds the photos on a phone and the files on a laptop.
It keeps its contents when the power goes off, which is why data centers stack it by the crateful.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/USB_flash_drive.JPG/500px-USB_flash_drive.JPG|What SanDisk sells. Data centers buy the storage chips inside these by the tens of thousands.|Nrbelex · CC BY-SA 3.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USB_flash_drive.JPG

The instrument at work here is the long-term supply agreement.
It fixes volumes and prices years ahead of delivery.
Think of writing down next winter's heating bill on today's contract: whatever the market does, both sides trade at the number in that box.

## How much ground the contracts cover

Borrowing and deploying money has not been this cheap in three decades.

## What "easy" actually means

A financial conditions index bundles interest rates, corporate bond spreads, share prices and the dollar into a single number that answers one question: how hard is it to get money right now.

Think of it as the height of a doorstep across the whole market.
When the step is low, borrowing is easy, and buying something with that borrowed money is easy too.

Two things pushed the index up.
Equities hit all-time highs, and corporate bond spreads stayed near their tightest since 1998.
A spread is the extra yield a weaker borrower must pay above government debt, so a low spread means lenders are barely pricing in the risk of not being repaid.

## The other set of numbers from the same week

@@CHK@@Labour force participation (July)|61.4%|Full-time employed (July)|133.55 million|High-yield spread (Aug 13)|2.71 points@@The first two are down 0.7 percentage points and 888,000 since January. Participation measures the share of working-age Americans who either hold a job or are looking for one.
People who stop looking drop out of the unemployment count too, so the unemployment rate never shows them.
July saw 264,000 leave, June 720,000, and since last November the total exceeds 2.4 million.

Households are moving the same way.
Credit card delinquencies of 90 days or more stood at 12.9% in the second quarter, the second-highest reading since the first quarter of 2011.
The post-crisis peak was 13.7%, so this is not far from it.
Student loan delinquencies are at 10.6%, the highest since early 2020, and auto loans at 5.5%, the second-highest on record.

## Where the easy money went

@@SHARE@@Nvidia|10 points|10|Apple, Microsoft, Broadcom, Alphabet|about 15 points|15|The other 495 stocks|about 59 points|59@@Five names produced roughly 25 of the 84 percentage points the S&P 500 returned over five years, close to 30% of the total. Easy money did not lift the market evenly; it crowded into a narrow strip.@@The Kobeissi Letter post, 2026-08-15 · retrieved 2026-08-16

Other figures from the same week lean the same way.
The share of US consumers expecting higher share prices a year out reached 41.4% in July, the highest since April 2021, and speculative long dollar positioning hit 48 billion dollars, the largest since 2015 after quadrupling in three months.

Expectations and positions swelled on the asset side; delinquencies and participation gave way on the household side.
Same country, same week.

## JOLTS, measured by a 30% response rate

One more thing sits underneath all of this.
The surveys that produce those labour numbers are not being answered the way they once were.
Kobeissi reported on 15 August that only about one in four businesses now agree to take part in the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, and that roughly 30% file in time for the first estimate.

@@REF@@Federal Statistics: Stakeholders Said Jobs Report Generally Meets Their Needs, but Opportunities Exist to Improve Data Quality (US Government Accountability Office, GAO-26-107538, 2026-06-02)|https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-107538|https://www.gao.gov/assets/extracts/3634bdab0eb31cd0d8c37cb3b0d3f3a9/rId25_image6.png

Its conclusion, though, is more careful than Kobeissi's.
For the household survey it recorded internal assessments finding limited effects on accuracy.
For the establishment survey it recorded that the Bureau of Labor Statistics has not yet released its assessment.
Participation comes from the household survey; job openings come from the establishment survey.
The side without a published assessment is the side markets stared at hardest this week.

So the contradiction runs two layers deep.
Easy money against strained households is one layer.
One of the two instruments measuring those households having no published verification is the second.
If participation slips further from here into the September FOMC and card delinquencies climb with it, easy financial conditions are running on a separate track from the real economy; if either one turns back, this exit reads as a single summer.

The firms that count the same strait with satellites and ship signals report numbers far below that.

@@BAR@@Normal traffic (first half of 2025)|20.9 million barrels a day|2090|Energy Secretary's seven-day average|9 million barrels a day|900|Kpler figure cited by Hanke (week of August 3)|1.74 million barrels a day|174@@All three numbers describe the same strait. @@CMP@@The Secretary's reading|Count everything leaving the Gulf. Add the 5 to 7 million barrels a day moving through new bypass pipelines to what crosses the strait and the total is not far from pre-war levels.|The ship-trackers' reading|Count only the vessels that actually transit. The largest single line in the Secretary's arithmetic is the oil that skips the strait entirely.
Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline can nominally push 7 million barrels a day across the country.

The Red Sea terminal at Yanbu where that oil is loaded, however, can only handle 4.5 to 5 million barrels a day.
A wide pipe into a narrow port exports at the rate of the port.

The Emirati line to Fujairah currently runs 1.8 million barrels a day, and the work to roughly double it is about half finished, targeted at 2027.
That is why Johnston measures actual pipeline throughput at around 4 million barrels a day.

@@REF@@Gulf states race to build Hormuz bypass infrastructure (Kpler, 2026-07-10)|https://www.kpler.com/blog/new-pipelines-bypassing-the-strait-of-hormuz-could-come-online-in-1-2-years|https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65059ad784ac02253c62356c/6a58b9d872b4d22f22e4a70d_thumbnail_Strait_of_Hormuz_77077bdae8.jpg

## August 14, and two Emirati tankers

Hanke wrote that 56 tankers crossed the strait on August 14 last year and 4 crossed on the same date this year.
That single day's count cannot be verified from public data, but what happened that day can.

@@REF@@UAE accuses Iran of attacks on two state oil company vessels in the Strait of Hormuz (Al Jazeera, 2026-08-14)|https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/14/uae-accuses-iran-of-attacks-on-two-adnoc-vessels-in-strait-of-hormuz|https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/getty_6a7e5499b4-1786664089.jpg?resize=1920%2C1440

The thin traffic is not a quirk of the statistics. It is attached to what happened on the water.

The price of passage tells the same story.
War risk premiums that ran at a quarter of one percent of hull value before the conflict now run between 3% and 10%.
For a $200 million tanker that is millions of dollars in premium for a single voyage, which means owners are staying away not because the channel is blocked but because the arithmetic no longer works.

So the argument is less about who is right than about which number you plan the next quarter around.
If Kpler's weekly average climbs above 9 million barrels a day before the end of the fourth quarter, the Secretary's account is supported; if it stays under that line through the quarter, the ship data was the better guide.

The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey draws a sample of 21,000 establishments and collects answers over about 45 days.

One opening for every unemployed worker.
This is one of the ratios the Federal Reserve is known to reach for when it asks whether the labor market is running hot, and job openings are the numerator.

The BLS budget was $636 million in fiscal 2025.
The fiscal 2026 request came in at $580 million, down 11.8%, and the same document carries a plan to cut staff by 17%.

Consumer price collection stopped in Lincoln, Nebraska and Provo, Utah in April 2025, and in Buffalo, New York in May.
Three hundred and fifty detailed producer price indexes were dropped, and two federal advisory committees that watched over economic statistics were closed in March 2025.

Since March 13, 2026 the BLS has been publishing the response-rate series for the job openings survey in its public database.

July job openings arrive on September 1, and June gets corrected the same day.
If the correction is smaller than 57,000, the late answers cannot move the first print much.
If it is bigger, then a market that has been reading each first print at face value has been trading a different number every month.
Either way, the thing worth watching is not how high job openings are. It is how far the figure travels afterwards.

elerian-blanchard-france-multiple-equili:
The expectation that the European Central Bank will buy your government bonds comes with conditions that are written down.
The first one is not being subject to an excessive deficit procedure, or, if subject to one, not being assessed as having failed to take effective action in response to a Council recommendation.
France has been subject to that procedure since July 2024.

@@REF@@The Transmission Protection Instrument (European Central Bank press release, 2022-07-21)|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pr/date/2022/html/ecb.pr220721~973e6e7273.en.html|https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/shared/img/socialmedia/social-default.jpg?0ef1632c35edede913681bb76af694a4

The reason this comes up now is a post Olivier Blanchard wrote on August 15 about France's public finances, which Mohamed El-Erian passed along with the note that the framework fits some other economies too.

## What the phrase multiple equilibria points at

Multiple equilibria describes a situation in which the same conditions can produce two different outcomes.
If investors believe the debt is safe, rates stay low and it can indeed be serviced; if they believe it is unsafe, rates rise and servicing really does become hard.
Belief produces the outcome.

It works like a run on a bank.
If everyone thinks the money is there, it is; if everyone goes to withdraw at once, it genuinely is not.

@@FLOW@@Safe zone|Debt is clearly serviceable and the central bank has nothing to do|Danger zone|A good outcome and a bad one sit side by side, and the bad one is avoided if the central bank buys when private investors sell|Default zone|Debt is clearly not serviceable, fiscal policy has to be adjusted first, and this is not the central bank's job@@Each zone calls for a different response, so not knowing which one you are standing in means not being able to pick the response.

This is where Blanchard puts his finger.
When investors demand a higher risk premium, the central bank does not know for sure whether this is the danger zone, where it should step in, or already the default zone, where absent an adjustment programme it should not.
So it leans toward asking for the programme first, and counting on it to remove the bad equilibrium on its own, he wrote, is unwise.

## Which zone France is standing in

@@BAR@@France|117.6%|117.6|Italy|138.9%|138.9|Euro area average|88.9%|88.9|Germany|64.4%|64.4@@Countries sharing one currency sit this far apart. That is why no single number draws the line where the danger zone begins.@@Retrieved 2026-08-15 · Eurostat government debt release (2026-07-21) · Q1 2026

@@REF@@Government debt in the euro area, first quarter of 2026 (Eurostat, 2026-07-21)|https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-euro-indicators/w/2-21072026-ap|https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/2995521/18500178/New Africa_AdobeStock_521389990_RV.jpg/6d6a3c42-5eb3-03d6-555d-a19fafaa1117

The rating agencies have moved one way.
Moody's cut in December 2024, Fitch followed in September 2025 and S&P in October 2025.
France now carries A+ at S&P and Fitch, and one notch above that at Moody's, which is the only one attaching a negative outlook.
That is not the rating of a country facing default, and it is not a rating that tells you the country is in the safe zone either.
It is closest to the middle of Blanchard's three zones, and the middle is precisely the one where the answer is not settled.

## The four lines written on July 21, 2022

When the ECB created a purchase tool called the Transmission Protection Instrument on July 21, 2022, it published four eligibility criteria alongside it.
Compliance with the EU fiscal framework, the absence of severe macroeconomic imbalances, debt sustainability, and sound and sustainable macroeconomic policies.

The first criterion reads as not being subject to an excessive deficit procedure, or not being assessed as having failed to take effective action in response to an EU Council recommendation.
France entered that procedure on July 26, 2024, and on January 21, 2025 the Council adopted a recommendation to correct the deficit by 2029.
The European Commission's compliance report of June 3, 2026 still lists France among the countries with an open procedure.

The conjunction in that sentence carries weight.
Being subject to the procedure does not by itself remove eligibility; eligibility survives if the country is assessed as taking effective action.
France's standing therefore rests with the Commission's assessment rather than with the ECB.
Where Blanchard expects the central bank to ask for an adjustment programme first, he is restating something already set down as a condition.

No instance of the instrument actually being activated could be found.
That it has stood unused for four years is itself part of what has held markets in place.

How much of an expectation that the central bank will buy belongs in the price of the bonds is what splits here.
Fitch reviews France again on August 28.
If the rating holds, the ground stays where it is; one notch lower and the market starts reading the conditions instead.

## What comes due on June 22, 2028

Block 7 sits on a sedimentary basin that begins south of Jeju Island.
It lies closer to Japan by distance, but the continental shelf under it runs back toward Korea, and in 1974 the two countries agreed to develop it together and split anything they found down the middle.
The agreement entered into force on June 22, 1978, for a term of fifty years.

@@REF@@Future of Korea-Japan joint development zone in doubt (Korea JoongAng Daily, 2024-02-14)|https://www.koreajoongangdaily.com/korea/future-of-korea-japan-joint-development-zone-in-doubt/11509987|https://image.koreajoongangdaily.com/11510171.jpg?imageId=11510171&panox=0&panoy=0&panow=0&panoh=0&width=1200&height=683

Japan did not give it that day, according to Yomiuri.

## Reading again the judgment that told Japan to wait

The original post locates Japan's patience in case law.
Natural prolongation, under which the country the shelf runs back to holds the rights, was the dominant doctrine into the 1970s, and the account has the International Court of Justice overturning that in the 1985 Libya-Malta case by ruling for a median line.

Open the judgment and the step does not land there.
The Court declined Malta's argument that equidistance had to be the mandatory starting point, and wrote that natural prolongation and distance are complementary rather than exclusive.
The drift is real: within 200 nautical miles, geological prolongation carries less legal weight than it once did.
What is not in that judgment is a sentence settling the question on a median line.
What kept Japan waiting is a probability leaning one way, not a decided rule.

There is a second place the original does not go.
China and Japan already agreed, in 2008, to develop this same stretch of sea jointly.

@@REF@@Delving deeper: China tests new waters in East China Sea oil and gas (CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative)|https://amti.csis.org/delving-deeper-china-tests-new-waters-in-east-china-sea-oil-and-gas/|https://amti.csis.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/North-ECS-jack-up-April-5-2026-banner.jpg

That agreement has gone eighteen years without being operationalised, and in the meantime China put its platforms up on the west side of the median line.
Signing something and then running out the clock has already produced one result in this water.

## The path by which Block 7 becomes disputed water

@@FLOW@@June 22, 2028|The Korea-Japan joint development agreement lapses after fifty years|Undelimited water|Neither side is left with settled ground to work it alone|One more party|China gains a place to argue, on natural prolongation, that it holds a share too@@What Japan may gain by waiting is not an exclusive licence but a sea with one more country in the arithmetic.

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is crude stored in 61 salt caverns at four sites on the Gulf Coast.
When war or a supply break leaves the market short, the president opens it and lets barrels out.

## The reserve has been the price tool

Oil has been climbing since the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed in late February, and this store of crude is what Washington reached for.

@@REF@@US strategic oil stockpile nears four-decade low as Iran war drags on (Al-Monitor, 2026-06-11)|https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/06/us-strategic-oil-stockpile-nears-four-decade-low-iran-war-drags|https://www.al-monitor.com/sites/default/files/styles/social_media_share/public/2026-06/GettyImages-2280782890.jpg

That report noted the reserve draining steadily as the war stretched on.
In the two months since, it has fallen further and set a fresh four-decade low.

On August 14 West Texas Intermediate settled at $82.40 a barrel and Brent at $88.52.
Gasoline averaged $4.07 a gallon nationally on August 15.
Barrels went into the market from the reserve, and prices are still here.

## Lent out rather than bought back

Here is the piece the original post leaves out.
There are two ways for the government to put crude back in the caverns.
One is a purchase, paid for out of budget. The other is an exchange, where refiners take barrels now and return barrels later.

@@TIME@@January 7, 1983|294.8 million barrels, back when the reserve was still being built up|January 2010|726.6 million barrels, the all-time peak|November 12, 2025|The Energy Department awards contracts to buy back 1 million barrels|June 10, 2026|Fifth solicitation under the 172-million-barrel release, repaid in barrels rather than cash@@It took 27 years to fill. Emptying it did not take nearly as long.@@EIA weekly stocks series and US Department of Energy press releases dated 2025-11-12 and 2026-06-10. Retrieved 2026-08-16.

The last confirmed cash purchase was in November 2025, for 1 million barrels.
Set against the capacity of the caverns, that is a corner of one room.

An exchange is a different animal.
The solicitation posted on June 10 covered 40 million barrels, with refiners taking crude now and returning crude later.
In earlier exchanges, borrowers repaid roughly 26% more than they took.

From the lender's side, it is a way to refill without spending a dollar of budget.
From the borrower's side, it is a bet that expensive oil today will be cheaper oil on the day the barrels have to go back.
Which means refilling the reserve now rides on the future oil price rather than on an appropriation.

## The 125 days the Energy Department cited

The mechanical numbers are simple.
Even after a presidential order it takes 13 days for the crude to reach the market, and no more than 4.4 million barrels a day can be pulled out however urgent it gets.
Members of the International Energy Agency are required to hold reserves equal to 90 days of net imports.
The Energy Department said that at 411 million barrels, where the reserve stood at the end of 2025, the SPR alone covered 125 days.
How many days it covers at today's level is not something published data shows.

The split is whether the barrels that went out on exchange come back as barrels.
If they do, the United States refills the caverns without spending tax money and gets its instrument back before the next supply shock.
If they do not, or if oil spikes again first, the country meets that moment with nothing left to sell into the market.
The question then is not what the price is. It is whether the government still has anything to put against it.

## What making a substrate out of glass means

A semiconductor die does not attach to a motherboard bare.
A thin plate goes in between to carry signals and power across, and today that plate is mostly built from plastic based material.

Switch that plate to glass and it gets thinner while using power more efficiently.
It also warps less under heat, which suits AI accelerators that spread several dies across a wide area.
The TrendForce piece above puts the gain at 25 percent less thickness and more than 30 percent better power efficiency.
The reason it gives for moving is cost. CoWoS, the method used today to tie dies together across a wide area, now runs at a per-unit price on a par with a 7nm class wafer.

## The step that is stuck is not the making

@@FLOW@@Glass blank|A flat panel much like display glass arrives|Drilling|Fine holes linking top to bottom are cut with a laser|Wiring and mounting|Metal fills the holes and circuitry is drawn on|Customer reliability testing|The customer applies heat and stress to see whether it cracks@@Of the four steps, the one that binds is the last. The maker can be ready and the date still moves, because the buyer has to sign off.

When Samsung Electro-Mechanics revised its start to 2028 at the late July second quarter briefing, the reason it gave was customer reliability testing of its prototypes.
Two companies are stuck at the same step.

Glass is hard, and hard things break.

Run heat up and down a panel drilled through with fine holes and cracks can start around those holes.
That is exactly what the customer is testing for.
A verdict arrives only after hundreds of cycles of mounting a die and taking the temperature up and back down.
The plant sits built and waiting through all of it.
That is why the schedule does not move at the maker's pace.

## The new date is the first half of 2027

The rule that has the Fed target an average of 2% in order to make up for past low inflation does not exist right now.
The Fed deleted that sentence from its statement on August 22, 2025.

On August 14 Peter Schiff took the rule to be alive and worked out a sum from it.
Inflation has averaged 4% over the past 65 months, so bringing the average back to 2% would take 65 months at 0%.

@@TIME@@2020-08-27|The Fed introduced average inflation targeting at Jackson Hole|2025-08-22|Powell said the Fed had returned to flexible inflation targeting and eliminated the makeup strategy|2026-01-27|The FOMC reaffirmed a statement identical to the August 2025 version|2026-08-14|Schiff published the 65-month sum, resting it on the average 2% target@@The rule the sum rests on left the statement about a year before the sum was written.@@Retrieved 2026-08-15 · Federal Reserve, Powell speech (2025-08-22) · Federal Reserve, FOMC press release (2026-01-27)

## What making up was supposed to mean

Average inflation targeting, adopted in August 2020, was a promise to read the target over a stretch of time rather than at a moment.
If inflation ran below the target for a while, it would be allowed to run above it for a while afterwards so that the average came out right.

@@REF@@What do changes in the Fed's longer-run goals and monetary strategy statement mean? (Brookings, 2020-09-02)|https://www.brookings.edu/articles/what-do-changes-in-the-feds-longer-run-goals-and-monetary-strategy-statement-mean/|https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/shutterstock_117869614.jpg?quality=50&w=500

Brookings, writing when the framework was new, described a promise with no period attached to it.
Inflation undershooting "for a time" would be answered by overshooting "for some time", and how many months went into the average was left open.
Powell himself called it a flexible form of average inflation targeting.
Because the averaging window was never pinned down, the stretch to be repaid does not fall out of the rule on its own.

## What the Fed said on the day the sentence went

On August 22, 2025, presenting the results of the framework review, Powell said the Fed had returned to flexible inflation targeting and eliminated the makeup strategy.
In the same remarks he said there had been nothing intentional or moderate about the inflation that arrived.

@@REF@@Speech by Chair Powell on the economic outlook and framework review (Federal Reserve Board, 2025-08-22)|https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/powell20250822a.htm|https://www.federalreserve.gov/images/social-media/social-default-image-opengraph.jpg

What went was not a phrase but the ground the sum stands on.
With a makeup clause, past inflation stays on the books as a debt to be repaid.
Without one, 2% from here is enough.
Then on January 27, 2026, at its annual organisational meeting, the FOMC reaffirmed a statement identical to the August 2025 version.
It has stayed deleted for close to a year.

## The arithmetic that survives January 27, 2026

The quarrel is not with the stretch Schiff measured or the average he found.
It is with where those values get entered.

Under the rule as it stands, five years of past inflation is a record rather than a balance owed.
So the sum reads better as a note on what the Fed has decided not to do than as a forecast of what it will do.
Had the makeup clause survived, today's price level would be a reason to hold rates high for years; with it deleted, that reason no longer comes out of the statement.
Whether the Fed turns back toward repaying the past is decided at the next framework review.

## Why prices rather than jobs

The sentiment index comes in two parts.
One asks how a household is doing now, the other asks how it expects to be doing.

The expectations half fell by more.
Had the drop come from fear of losing work, the half that asks about present circumstances should have moved first and moved harder.
The original post noted that concern about employment stayed relatively low.

The survey holds one more number that shows what kind of decline this is.
Asked whether their own income will rise faster than prices over the coming year, 8% said yes.
In December 2024, 18% said yes to the same question.
Fewer than one household in ten now expects to end the year better off.

## What four weeks did to the price of gasoline

Asked how much prices will rise over the next year, respondents answered 4.3%, a little above July's 4.2%.
The five-to-ten-year answer stayed at 3.3%, unchanged from July.
The distant future held still while the coming year moved.

Inflation expectations track the prices people see most often.
In the United States, the price seen most often is the number on the sign outside a filling station.
The national average price of gasoline rose from $3.855 a gallon on July 13 to $4.006 on August 10.

@@REF@@US consumers sour on economy as inflation concerns remain in focus, UMich survey says (Yahoo Finance, 2026-08-14)|https://www.aol.com/articles/us-consumers-sour-economy-inflation-144047000.html|https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/14/d06481c0-11d0-3dab-81b2-59fa44bc65e5/5c2cc9ab-c0ac-400a-b126-926048bd35e3.jpg

Survey director Joanne Hsu said the weakening reached across demographic groups but that the largest reductions came among older consumers, lower-income consumers and those without a college degree.
When the price of something a household cannot stop buying goes up, the households where that item takes the biggest share of the budget shake first.
The cost-of-living explanation in the original post points the right way, but it leaves one step out. What lifted that cost of living is fuel that came through the Middle East conflict.

## What to watch in Michigan's final August reading

A low sentiment index and falling consumption are not the same statement.
The index carries how people feel about prices as well, so a decline pushed by prices and a decline pushed by job losses arrive as the same number.

If the final August reading due at the end of the month settles below the 51.0 preliminary, this drop is confirmed; if it climbs back above 51.0, the preliminary overshot.
The number to read alongside it is the 4.3% year-ahead inflation expectation. If that rises further with gasoline, prices are holding sentiment down; if it falls back below that level, the shock of early August was a one-month affair.

## The test for the top bracket is weight and heat

Two things put a drone in the top bracket.
One is a maximum take-off weight above 25kg, roughly 55 pounds.
The other is thermal imaging.

A hobby camera drone usually weighs around a kilogram, so it does not meet either test.
What does is the airframe carrying pesticide over a field, the one hauling materials, and the one that can see the heat of people and equipment at night.
Weight and heat, taken together, are a net for catching airframes that could be used for military or surveillance work.
Docking stations, which drones need in order to take off and land unattended, and critical components fall into the same bracket.

## What it takes to sit in the allied bracket

There is a separate bracket with lower rates.
The European Union, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland and Liechtenstein get 15%, and the United Kingdom gets 10%.

@@REF@@Fact sheet: imposing tariffs on drones and their parts and components (The White House, 2026-08-13)|https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/08/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-bolsters-national-security-and-strengthens-u-s-supply-chains-by-imposing-tariffs-on-drones-and-their-parts-and-components/|https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/WH47-Social-Share-Card.jpg

The rate comes with a condition. The White House fact sheet says substantially all of the hardware, the software and the technology has to originate in that country or in the United States.
A drone does not fly on its airframe alone. Flight control software, maps and communication modules come with it.
So an aircraft assembled in Korea or Japan still misses the lower bracket if the software inside it fails the origin test.

## American makers pass through the same gate

The original post read the move as good news for US drone component suppliers and aircraft makers.
The direction is right, but one bracket is missing from that reading.
The 25% rate covers a broad set of components, and American manufacturers import a great many of them.
The proclamation gives 180 days to non-sensitive components and to products carrying Department of War or FCC exemptions.
That builds a six-month gap between the moment costs rise and the moment domestic production is meant to stand up.
The same proclamation directs the commerce secretary to set up an onshoring incentive programme, which reads as a device for filling that gap.

## What splits after September 3

What splits here is whether this tariff raises American drone revenue or American drone costs.
If US airframes fill the space that the top tariff clears of imported finished drones, revenue moves first.
If procurement costs rise by the tariff before that, margin moves first.
If gross margins at US drone makers rise from the prior quarter in the first results after September 3, it is the former; if they fall, it is the latter.

## The chip at the bottom of HBM

HBM is memory built by stacking eight to twelve DRAM dies vertically.
At the very bottom sits one more die that is not DRAM.
It marshals the signals the stacked DRAM sends and receives and pushes them out of the package. It is called the base die.

A base die is logic, not memory.
So it is made on a foundry process rather than in a DRAM plant.
Until now a 4nm-class process was enough, but as stacks got taller and speeds higher, heat became the problem.
Doing the same work on less power calls for a finer process, and the answer being floated is 2nm.

## Where the wafers travel

The arrangement described in the report is a "send fab".
Rather than building a product end to end, such a line takes in wafers from other production lines, runs one specific stretch of the process, and sends them back.

@@FLOW@@Production line|Wafers come off Samsung's foundry production lines|NRD-K Line 2|The handed-over wafers get their base die patterned on a 2nm process|HBM stacking|Eight to twelve DRAM dies are stacked on top and bound into one package|Customer|It ships to AI accelerator makers such as NVIDIA@@Once the base die moves to 2nm, what sets HBM's speed is the foundry process, not the DRAM process.

This is where the news actually bites.
The memory contest is shifting from a race to shrink DRAM into a race for a slot on the newest foundry node.
2nm is the node where smartphone application processors and AI chips are already queueing. Memory now wants to join that queue.

Earlier reporting says HBM5 is expected to run more than 50% faster than HBM4E.
Samsung has said it will spend 20 trillion won building three NRD-K lines by 2030.
One of those three would be changing jobs.

## What one NRD-K line costs

A research line is where the next generation gets tested.
Turn it over to production and the orders in front of you get filled, but the test bench for the generation after that loses a slot.
This is still at the review stage, and the company has announced nothing.

What splits here is whether Samsung fights the HBM war as a memory company or as a company that owns a foundry.
If it absorbs the 2nm base die in-house, it finishes inside its own walls the step SK Hynix hands to TSMC.
If Line 2 instead starts up as planned for research and development, this report stays a report.
